profile_summary: This respondent tends to see observed gender differences as mostly shaped by individual personality, opportunity, and social expectations rather than reflecting basic differences between men and women. They allow some room for differences in areas like interests, emotional expression, or physical abilities, but generally believe the underlying capacities and approaches are more similar than different.

This respondent sees gender differences as shaped mainly by social roles and interests: men and women often gravitate toward different hobbies, parenting styles, and workplace strengths, but are not fundamentally different in basic physical capacity or in how openly they can express emotions.

This profile sees broad overlap between men and women in personal interests and what they can physically do, especially given individual variation and opportunity. At the same time, it perceives gendered social expectations as shaping more noticeable differences in parenting style, emotional expression, and the kinds of strengths people tend to bring to workplace tasks.

This respondent sees men and women as often shaped by different social expectations in everyday life, especially in interests, parenting roles, and emotional expression. At the same time, they are skeptical that these differences imply broad limits in physical capability or workplace competence, viewing people as largely similar in what they can do when given comparable opportunities.

This respondent sees men and women as often shaped by different social expectations and tendencies in interests, emotional expression, physical strengths, and workplace aptitudes, while still believing that caregiving and parenting approaches are largely rooted in similar concerns and responsibilities.

This respondent sees broad overlap in people's interests, bodies, and caregiving styles, emphasizing individual variation over gender categories. At the same time, they think social norms and expectations still shape how men and women tend to show emotions and the kinds of strengths they develop or display at work.

This respondent sees many everyday preferences and competencies as shaped more by individual personality, opportunity, and social context than by gender, leading them to view hobbies, emotional expression, and workplace strengths as broadly similar. At the same time, they think physical capacities often differ on average and that parenting roles or instincts can still be meaningfully shaped by gendered expectations or experiences.

This respondent sees broad overlap between men and women in personal interests, parenting values, and everyday physical capabilities, while still believing that socialization and expectations often lead men and women to express emotions differently and develop somewhat different workplace strengths.

This respondent sees many everyday differences as shaped by social interests and occupational sorting, so hobbies and workplace strengths often appear gendered. At the same time, they think men and women are broadly alike in core capacities, caregiving instincts, and emotional expression when given similar expectations and opportunities.

This respondent sees many everyday preferences and modes of self-presentation as shaped by gendered socialization, leading them to expect differences in hobbies, physical abilities, and emotional expression. At the same time, they think caregiving values and workplace competence are broadly shared across men and women, with individual variation mattering more than gender in those areas.

This respondent sees most everyday preferences and caregiving or emotional behaviors as shaped more by individual personality and shared social roles than by gender, but still believes average physical capacities and some work-related strengths often differ between men and women.

This respondent sees many everyday interests and parenting styles as shaped by gendered socialization, but believes that men and women have broadly overlapping capacities in physical activity, emotional expression, and workplace competence.

This respondent sees many observed differences as domain-specific rather than universal: hobbies and parenting often diverge because of social expectations and life roles, while physical abilities, emotional expression, and workplace strengths vary more by individual than by gender.

This respondent generally emphasizes overlap and individual variation in interests, physical capacity, and emotional expression, but still believes social expectations and typical role experiences lead men and women to approach parenting and workplace strengths differently.

This respondent generally sees men and women as having broad overlap in interests, capabilities, parenting styles, and workplace strengths, viewing most differences as individual rather than gender-based. However, they think social expectations still lead men and women to express emotions in noticeably different ways.

This respondent emphasizes broad overlap between men and women in everyday interests, general capabilities, and caregiving approaches, while still perceiving noticeable gendered patterns in emotional expression and in the kinds of strengths people are encouraged to develop at work.
